This is why meta-analysis is nice but can't be taken entirely serious because the details are important and we barely have the whole story. They also mention only looking specifically at time spent on the one specific task, and didn't mention related tasks practiced (which seems extremely important for things such as sports, music, etc...)

I see a lot of variables not accounted for(though it is obviously hard to see as I can't look through all the hundreds of papers involved) and a decent amount of subjectivity.

Did you read the full paper or just the abstract? I've found that the conclusions or summary detailed in the abstract rarely match up with the actual research.

This meta analysis seems questionable at best. Of the 157 studies that met their criteria, 10 showed a negative correlation between deliberate practice and performance - meaning the player who practice more does worse!

They also mix in all results whereas deliberate practice is something that depends heavily on the skill level of the practitioners. For instance for individuals that have already achieved mastery and have trained the necessary muscle memory and so on - deliberate practice is not going to show big gains. A competitor at a high base skill level is going to show a far better performance than a less skilled player even with negligible deliberate practice. That doesn't mean they didn't practice their asses off to get their level in the first place.

I mean the paper is interesting, but I'm not sure you can actually draw any meaningful conclusions from its results.
